lesson.title: Non-REM Sleep: The Body's Quiet Repair Shift
lesson.summary: Non-REM sleep, spanning the three lighter and deeper stages that precede each REM period, is when the body does most of its physical restoration and the brain consolidates factual, everyday memories.
lesson.body:
Non-REM sleep refers collectively to the three stages introduced earlier in this chapter, N1, N2, and N3, that make up the majority of a typical night's sleep and occur before each period of REM sleep within the roughly ninety-minute sleep cycle. Where REM sleep is defined by a brain that looks almost awake on an EEG recording, non-REM sleep moves in the opposite direction: brain wave activity generally slows and becomes larger in amplitude the deeper a person sleeps, reaching its slowest and largest form during stage three, or slow-wave sleep. This contrast between an active, dreaming brain during REM and a quieter, slower brain during non-REM is one of the most fundamental distinctions in sleep science.

The physiological state of the body during non-REM sleep also differs sharply from both wakefulness and REM sleep. The parasympathetic nervous system, responsible for calming and restorative bodily functions, becomes dominant, and heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing rate all slow down and become notably more regular than during either waking hours or REM sleep. Body temperature drops slightly as well, part of an overall physiological pattern oriented toward conserving energy and supporting repair rather than readiness for action.

Slow-wave sleep, the deepest portion of non-REM sleep, appears to be especially important for physical restoration. It is during this stage that the anterior pituitary gland, discussed earlier in this chapter, releases the largest pulses of growth hormone, which supports tissue repair, muscle growth, and, in children and adolescents, physical growth itself. This connection helps explain why chronic short or disrupted sleep, which reduces time spent in slow-wave sleep, has been linked to problems with physical recovery and immune function, since a key hormonal signal for repair is disproportionately tied to this particular sleep stage rather than being released steadily throughout the night.

Non-REM sleep, and slow-wave sleep in particular, also plays an important role in memory, but of a different flavor than the memory functions associated with REM sleep. Declarative memory, meaning memory for facts and specific events, such as remembering a new vocabulary word or the details of a conversation from earlier in the day, appears to benefit substantially from slow-wave sleep, during which patterns of neural activity from waking experience seem to be replayed and gradually strengthened, helping shift information from a fragile, temporary form into more stable long-term storage.

Non-REM sleep, particularly its deepest stage, is also the stage most associated with certain unusual sleep behaviors known as parasomnias. Sleepwalking and night terrors, for example, typically arise from a partial, incomplete arousal out of deep slow-wave sleep rather than during REM, which is part of why a sleepwalker's eyes may be open and their movements coordinated even though they remain largely unresponsive and typically have no memory of the episode afterward. This stands in useful contrast to nightmares, which are vivid frightening dreams that occur during REM sleep. Together, the distinct physiological and cognitive contributions of non-REM sleep complement those of REM sleep, underscoring that a full night of healthy sleep depends on cycling properly through both kinds of brain states rather than favoring one over the other.
